Motivation

Tangible controls need wires, a phone close by, or markers

  1. 1TUIs provide tactile and proprioceptive feedback
  2. 2embedded circuits that need power to function
  3. 3smartphone sensors like magnetometers, IMUs, and touchscreens
  4. 4Fiducial markers, such as QR codes, ArUco markers, and AprilTag
  5. 5a vision-based TUI that enables high-precision tracking of passive widgets

State of the art

No passive control was both far and precise

  1. 1SlapWidgets and reacTIVision use a camera and projector setup to track tangibles on interactive surfaces
  2. 2RFID techniques show promise, the resolution is low, sensing is not continuous
  3. 3MoiréWidgets can be used at greater distances while maintaining high-resolution sensing of interactions

It shows Older passive controls by how far off and how finely each can be read, and none was both far and fine.

How to read it Right is a longer reach, and up is a finer reading, down to less than a millimetre.

Background

Four terms used throughout

Moiré effect01

the light-dark-light pattern that emerges when two, dense, repetitive patterns are overlaid

Display window02

four colored square markers at the corners of the display window where the Moiré pattern is presentFor reliable tracking the window should hold at least three Moiré peaks (§3.4). The peaks repeat every Tm, the fringe period (§3.1): 7.8 mm in this model, from assumed layer periods.

Phase03

the Moiré fringes can be represented as a sinusoidal functionThe phase says where in its cycle that wave sits; it shifts as the fringes move.

Primitive movement04

MoiréWidgets convert user input into one of these three movements to track interactions

two layers and their fringes

It shows Two fine stripe patterns laid over each other make wide dark bands, the Moiré fringes.

How to read it Lower pattern fixed, upper one in its own colour; where their lines fall between each other the overlap goes dark.

the fringes as a wave

It shows What the camera reads: the fringes averaged into one wave, its crest marked, and its phase in degrees.

How to read it As the top layer moves, the crest slides along and the phase turns; that turn is the reading.

Core idea

A small move of the top layer sweeps the fringes far

  1. 1When two square waves of marginally varied frequencies overlap multiplicatively
  2. 2a combined wave of diverse frequencies called a Moiré pattern
  3. 3Movements orthogonal to the parallel lines generate a signal with higher sensitivity
  4. 4calculates the displacement from the phase shift of the fringes
the two layers and their fringes

It shows The two layers' lines and their overlap: in this model (assumed periods 0.65 and 0.60 mm) the fringes are 7.8 mm apart.

How to read it In this model, as the top layer slides 1 mm, the dark fringes slide 13 mm: the layer's move, magnified.

the fringes as a wave

It shows What the camera reads: the fringes averaged into one wave, its crest marked, and its phase in degrees.

How to read it As the top layer moves, the crest slides along and the phase turns; that turn is the reading.

Core idea · what to observe

The fringes move much farther than the layer

we form Moiré patterns responsive to subtle user movements

  1. Layer still: the fringes stay put
  2. The top layer slides 1 mm: the fringes sweep 13 mm (this model's periods)
  3. In this model the fringes repeat every 7.8 mm
  4. So a camera sees a big move, not a tiny one
Top layer moved –
Fringes moved –
the two layers and their fringes

It shows The two line layers over each other, and the fringes a camera sees: they move far more than the layer, 13 times in this model.

How to read it The marked line is the top layer's, the dashed one a fringe; the words at the right say how far each moved.

Challenge 1 · five motions

Each widget is moved in its own way

Sliders, buttons, and switches can be decomposed to a 1D movement since they require motion along a single axis

This type of design is naturally well-suited for creating dials

  1. Five widgets: pressed, flipped, slid, turned, pushed
  2. A press, a flip and a slide move along one line
  3. A joystick moves in a plane, a dial turns
  4. One pair of patterns cannot read them all

How to read it The lit box is the widget moving now; at the last click, yes or no says whether parallel lines can read it.

Solution 1 · three primitives

Three primitive movements, each with its own pattern pair

MoiréWidgets convert user input into one of these three movements

  1. New: the slider's two line layers slide into its housing
  2. The joystick: two grids, so its fringes move in x and y
  3. The dial: two radial patterns, so its fringes turn
  4. Your turn Pick a widget; drag, press or turn it

Challenge 2 · printed fringes

Consumer 3-D printers cannot print regular fringes

Consumer-grade 3D printers lack the precision and consistency to generate reliable Moiré patterns

The Moiré patterns are warped and irregular

  1. Printed by FDM: the line spacing wanders
  2. The fringes come out uneven and warped
  3. So the fitted phase drifts off the true move
Slider moved –
RMS error, full slide –
the layers as an FDM printer makes them

It shows FDM lines wander and bow, so the fringes are uneven and the fitted crest lands off where even lines put it: the reading drifts.

How to read it Top rows: each layer's lines; below, the fringes seen (solid), the sine fitted (dashed), its crest (red) and even lines' crest (grey).

Solution 2 · paper layers

Laser-printed layers on a 3-D printed body

we utilize 3D printing for the mechanical assemblies and use a laser paper printer to print the Moiré fringes

Lines that are too thin (less than 0.2 mm) produce a weaker Moiré signal, while excessively thick lines result in overly dark patterns

  1. New: laser-printed layers, the top on film, the bottom on sticker paper
  2. Even lines give even fringes, and the fit tracks the move
  3. Your turn Laser printing off and on; line width
RMS error, full slide –

the layers as printed

It shows Laser-printed lines are even, so the fringes are a clean wave and the fitted crest sits where it should: the error stays small.

How to read it Top rows: each layer's lines; below, the fringes (solid), the sine fitted (dashed), its crest (red) and even lines' crest (grey).

Challenge 3 · reading the frame

The fringes fill a small, tilted patch of the frame

identify the area where the Moiré pattern is present

  1. The camera sees the window small and tilted
  2. Read raw, its fine lines swamp the fringes
  3. So the phase read raw jumps about

Solution 3 · markers, warp, fit

Markers, a perspective warp, a blur and a sine fit

we place four colored square markers at the corners of the display window

we calculate the average intensity along the y-axis of the blurred image

  1. New: colour markers at the window's corners
  2. A perspective warp turns the window square on
  3. A blur and a mean along y leave one smooth wave
  4. A sine fit gives the phase; its change gives the move
  5. Your turn Pipeline off and on, then drag the slider

Check the Paper · 2 of 3

Ablation study

Question What does each stage of the image pipeline add to the reading?§3.5 reads the fringes in four stages (Fig. 5); the paper always runs all four. Here one is switched off at a time. The camera is at 100 cm, swung 30°, as in Fig. 7's 30°/0° panel.

You change
the pipeline's stages, one off at a time

Why it matters In this model a phase error inside one period is divided by the gain, but a miscounted period costs 0.65 mm.0.65 mm is one line period of the model's assumed layers. Each error follows the paper's test (the carriage moved up to 20 mm, here 20 mm, read at 25 frames), as the model's mean over seeded runs (24 at Fig. 7's settings, as its checks, 4 elsewhere).

  1. 1Your turn PressNo markers and no warp: the region stays where the window was in the first frame. The window then slides out of it, and the fringes are read in the camera's frame, not the window's.
  2. 2Your turn PressThe brightest peak's place stands in for the fit. One peak, read to a sample, jumps with the noise; the fit uses every sample of the window.
  3. 3Your turn PressEach frame's phase alone, with no sum over frames. In this model the phase repeats every 0.65 mm of travel (assumed periods), so the move is lost.

Generalization study

Question How far and how steep can the camera be before the reading fails?Fig. 7 tests 20 to 220 cm, and up to 60° in X and 30° in Z. Here the camera goes to 400 cm and 75°.

You change
the camera's distance and angle

Why it matters In this model, far away each pixel covers more of the window, so the markers' corners and the fringe's phase wander more.The paper reports the error growing, not why. The model unwraps to the nearest period (assumed): a frame's phase error past half a period counts a period wrong, 0.65 mm with its assumed layers.

  1. 1Your turn Take the camera to 400 cm.Fig. 7's last test is 220 cm at 0°/0°, where the paper's Moiré error is 4.2 mm. Past it the curve is the model's alone; the shaded part of the plot is past the paper's tests.
  2. 2Your turn Swing the camera to 75°.Swung toward X, the window looks shorter along the fringes by cos αX, so each fringe takes fewer pixels. The paper stops at 60° and left out 60° with a 30° tilt (§4.2).

Physical conditions

Question Which matters most: the camera, the pattern, the speed or the light?Each tab changes one thing the paper fixes, with the camera at 100 cm, 0°/0°. The paper's error there is 0.3 mm (Fig. 7).

You change
one condition, a tab each
CameraPatternSpeedLight
  1. 1Your turn Set the video to 720p, then to 4K.The paper records 1080p. At 720p each pixel covers 1.5 times as much of the window; at 4K half as much.
Error at 100 cm –
Pixels per fringe –

What you saw 720p and 4K are outside the paper's tests. The markers' corner noise is kept at 1.3 px of the frame, assumed.All recordings were in 1080p and made using an iPhone 11 Pro mounted on a tripod

  1. 1Your turn Widen the period difference to 0.1 mm.A wider dT makes shorter fringes, Tm = Ta·Tb/dT, and a smaller gain. With this model's assumed periods, below about 0.04 mm the 30 mm window holds fewer than 3 fringes.
  2. 2Your turn Thin the lines to 0.1 mm.Thin lines dim the fringes; lines that fill the period (0.6 mm in this model, assumed) leave no light between them.
Error at 100 cm –
Fringes in the window –
Gain –
Fringe contrast –

What you saw The model's fit knows the fringes' frequency, so fewer than 3 fringes cost it little; the paper asks for at least three (§3.4).Lines that are too thin (less than 0.2 mm) produce a weaker Moiré signal, while excessively thick lines result in overly dark patterns

  1. 1Your turn Speed the move up to 10 mm/s.The paper's Eq. 1 turns the phase change between two frames into travel, assuming under one period between them. This model unwraps to the nearest period (assumed), so its limit is half a period: 9.75 mm/s at 30 frames a second with its assumed 0.65 mm period.
Error at 100 cm –
Unwrap's speed limit –

What you saw The frame rate, 30 per second, is assumed. The carriage moves in jerks (assumed), so some frames pass the limit before the mean speed does.preventing the Moiré pattern from shifting by more than one period between the two frames

  1. 1Your turn Make the light uneven, σ 40.σ is in grey levels of 255, frame to frame and pixel to pixel. The markers' colour edge moves with it: one pixel more when σ equals their 45-level contrast, assumed.
Error at 100 cm –
Corner wander –

What you saw The paper names this failure and gives no number; the model's link from the light to the corners is assumed.The four colored markers at the corners of the printed fringes used to extract and process the Moiré pattern can fail under irregular lighting conditions, like dark shadows and bright highlights

Limits of this model

What This Model Leaves Open

Not modelled

Shown by the paper, not simulated here.

  1. The two design tools: an OnShape feature that places the widgets, and a GUI that makes the printed fringesdesign software; the model draws the patterns the tools export (the periods, the line thickness), not the tools themselves Fig. 4; §3.4
  2. SLA-printed fringes: the supports bond to and damage the fringesthe model simulates FDM's spacing error and warp (c2), not resin supports torn from the fringes Fig. 9B; §5.2
